title: Water at eye level
originalTitle: Lake Alice, University of Florida, Gainesville
author: Michael Rivera
alt: A grassy bank and moss-draped trees beside Lake Alice, with floating vegetation and open water beyond.
caption: A ground-level view of Lake Alice: lawn, overhanging branches, floating vegetation, and open water share the same scene.
question: What could a single satellite pixel contain here?
insight: The photograph makes mixed surfaces visible. A satellite pixel may combine water, leaves, and shade; an index value cannot separate all of those details.

title: Where forest meets water
author: Alexander Abair
alt: Tree trunks, palmettos, roots, and standing water at the wooded edge of Lake Alice.
caption: Water reaches between tree trunks at the wooded margin. This is a closer look at the overlap between the lake and its forested edge.
question: Is this patch simply water, or simply vegetation?
insight: The categories overlap on the ground. Canopy can hide water from an overhead image, and one photograph cannot establish the usual water level or a flooding trend.

title: Inside the canopy
author: Alexander Abair
alt: A wooden boardwalk leads through dense trees and palmettos toward sunlight at Lake Alice.
caption: A boardwalk threads through the woods toward Lake Alice. From below, the canopy becomes a layered space rather than a green patch.
question: Which parts of this path disappear from above?
insight: Ground photography reveals the understory and human access. LiDAR adds measured vertical structure, while a vegetation index describes reflected light at a much coarser scale.

title: Light changes the lake
author: Alexander Abair
alt: Orange and pink sunset clouds reflected in Lake Alice, framed by a dark tree line.
caption: Sunset colors reflect across Lake Alice. The apparent color of the water changes with the sky and lighting.
question: Does a different water color mean different water quality?
insight: Not by itself. This camera records visible light, not the near-infrared band needed for NDWI. Neither this photograph nor an NDWI value establishes water quality.
